lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.focus: survey, experiment, and observational study design
lessonRef.title: Discussion or problem seminar: survey, experiment, and observational study design

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: One approach is shown. There is at least one other that works.

items.prompt: n = 400, sample proportion 55%. Margin and interval?

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: For each, name a second method before you solve it.

items.prompt: In 1000 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 24 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 2.4% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 2.4% of simulations, which is not unusual.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 64 and standard deviation 3. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 58 and 70?
choices: about 99.7%
about 95%
about 50%
about 68%

items.prompt: A researcher runs an observational study of volunteers who chose their own group. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A random sample of 625 people gives a sample proportion of 74%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±8%, giving 66% to 82%
±4%, giving 70% to 78%
±74%, giving 0% to 148%

items.prompt: In 100 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 3 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 3% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 3% of simulations, which is not unusual.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 125 and standard deviation 10. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 115 and 135?
choices: about 95%
about 99.7%
about 68%
about 50%

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: Argue for one method over another. Say what makes it better, not just that it is.

items.prompt: A researcher runs a randomised controlled experiment with participants randomly assigned to treatments. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: A random sample of 625 people gives a sample proportion of 49%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
